content: Uterine fibroids are the most common benign tumors found in the uterus of women of reproductive age. Mifepristone (RU-486) works by competitively binding to and inhibiting progesterone receptors. Research has indicated that the growth of fibroids is influenced by sex steroids, and mifepristone has been shown to reduce the size of fibroids. This review evaluates the effects of mifepristone on fibroids and its associated adverse effects, as reported in randomized controlled trials. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of mifepristone in managing uterine fibroids in premenopausal women. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Review Group's specialized register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, up to November 2011. Additional searches included handsearching journals, reviewing reference lists, exploring databases of ongoing trials, and searching the internet. No language restrictions were applied. Only randomized controlled trials comparing mifepristone to other medical therapies or placebo in premenopausal women with confirmed uterine fibroids were included. Four authors independently extracted data and assessed the quality of the trials. Data were analyzed using Peto odds ratios (OR) for categorical data and weighted mean differences for continuous data, both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Meta-analyses were conducted using a fixed-effect model. Three studies, involving a total of 112 participants, were included in the review. The interventions compared included different dosages of mifepristone, placebo, and vitamin B tablets. Evidence from the studies demonstrated that mifepristone significantly reduced heavy menstrual bleeding compared to placebo (Peto OR 17.84; 95% CI 6.72 to 47.38; 2 RCTs, 77 women, I² = 0%). The meta-analysis included data from three studies (Bagaria 2009, Engman 2009, and Fiscella 2006). However, there was no evidence to suggest that mifepristone reduced fibroid volume (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.02; 95% CI -0.38 to 0.41; 99 women). Two studies (Bagaria 2009 and Fiscella 2006) contributed to this analysis. Similarly, there was no evidence of an effect on uterine volume (mean difference [MD] -77.24; 95% CI -240.62 to 86.14; 72 women). The pooled data indicated an increased risk of adverse events, specifically abnormal endometrial histology, in the mifepristone group compared to placebo (OR 31.65; 95% CI 4.83 to 207.35; 2 RCTs; 54 women; I² = 0%). One study (Bagaria 2009) reported cases of endometrial hyperplasia at the end of therapy, with 12 out of 19 women in the mifepristone group affected, compared to none in the placebo group (OR 55.0; 95% CI 2.86 to 105.67). Another study (Engman 2009) found a significantly higher rate of cystic glandular dilatation in the mifepristone group (5 out of 8 women biopsied) compared to the placebo group (1 out of 11 women biopsied) (OR 16.67; 95% CI 1.36 to 204.03). One study (Fiscella 2006) reported significant improvements in specific quality-of-life outcomes for women treated with mifepristone (P < 0.001). In conclusion, mifepristone was found to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding and improve fibroid-specific quality of life. However, it did not demonstrate a reduction in fibroid volume. Further well-designed and adequately powered randomized controlled trials are necessary before mifepristone can be recommended for the treatment of uterine fibroids.
